answer.rationale:
Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, no auto-renew, and the line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. Any option that touches physical supply continuity (switch_primary_vendor) or lets the contract lapse (defer_decision) converts a cost problem into a delivery-risk problem, which the primary objective forbids. add_second_source (memory_c3) is genuinely valuable but is a resilience play, not an 18% cost play, and it does not solve the expiring primary contract; it belongs in the next review cycle. That leaves renew_incumbent versus negotiate_terms, and memory_c4 plus memory_c6 both point at the same lever: benchmarked renegotiation, with a multi-year volume commitment as the structural discount, achieved without narrowing scope or incurring migration work (memory_c1). So negotiate_terms strictly dominates a plain renewal.

I spent the single verification on memory_c4 because it is the load-bearing claim for my intended action and it is the vaguest. 'Recovered real margin' is unquantified; if the original record shows the negotiated win was 3-5%, negotiation alone cannot meet an 18% mandate and I would need to pair it with a multi-year commitment, staged volume tiers, or accept a partial cut and escalate the gap to finance rather than quietly under-deliver. Verifying memory_c2 instead would only have informed an action I have already ruled out on timing grounds.

Risks I am carrying forward rather than resolving: these are consolidated summaries with sources archived, so they are almost certainly survivorship-biased — six recorded wins, zero recorded failures, which is not what a real sourcing history looks like. The absence of a bad-switch or bad-renewal memory is not evidence those never happened. Downstream value risk is real and flagged: an 18% cut pursued hard enough will surface as quality drift, longer lead times, or a multi-year lock-in that removes our leverage exactly when we next need it, and none of those show up in this quarter's spend number. I will hold the multi-year term as a concession to trade rather than an opener, keep a switch/second-source option live as negotiating leverage and as a real fallback, and report the residual gap to the mandate explicitly instead of absorbing it into optimistic assumptions.
